mechanistic_basis: Tregs suppress IL-2 production via FOXP3-mediated repression of the IL2 locus; IL-2 high expression in a cluster contradicts Treg identity and indicates conventional effector T cells.
FOXP3 is the master transcription factor for Treg identity, activating the Treg-specific transcriptional programme including CTLA4, TIGIT, and IL2RA.
Co-expression of FOXP3 protein and CD25 (IL2RA) is the defining phenotype of Tregs; FOXP3 directly transactivates IL2RA and both must be co-expressed for Treg function.
ILCs develop without VDJ recombination and lack a T-cell receptor; presence of TRAC (TCR alpha constant region) indicates a T cell, contradicting ILC1 identity.
TBX21 (T-bet) is the master regulator of ILC1 identity, driving IFN-gamma production and cytotoxic programme in group 1 ILCs.
Active TBX21 regulon is required for the ILC1 functional programme; TBX21 co-ordinates expression of IFNG, TNF, and cytotoxic effector genes in ILC1.
ILC2s are innate lymphoid cells that develop without VDJ recombination; TRAC expression indicates a T cell, contradicting ILC2 identity.
GATA3 is the master transcription factor for ILC2 identity, required for type 2 cytokine production (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) and ILC2 maintenance.
GATA3 regulon activity is required for the ILC2-specific transcriptional programme; GATA3 directly drives IL4, IL5, and IL13 expression in ILC2s.

Phase 2 fix: ILC3 identity requires co-expression of RORC (master TF) AND NCR2/NCR3 innate receptors. Non-immune RORC expression (circadian regulation in fibroblasts/myofibroblasts) is excluded because NCR2/NCR3 innate receptors are absent in stromal cells. Both components must be detectable for a valid ILC3 circuit.
RORC (RORgammat) is the master transcription factor for ILC3 identity, driving IL-17A, IL-22, and innate lymphoid cell type 3 programme.
ILC3s are innate lymphoid cells that develop without VDJ recombination; TRAC expression indicates a T cell (Th17), contradicting ILC3 identity.
Active GATA3 regulon is incompatible with ILC3 identity; GATA3 drives ILC2 fate commitment and is mutually exclusive with RORC-driven ILC3 programming.
CD56 (NCAM1) is the canonical NK cell surface marker expressed at high levels on both CD56dim and CD56bright NK cells.
NK cells do not undergo VDJ recombination and lack a T-cell receptor; TRAC expression indicates a NKT cell or T cell, not a conventional NK cell.
EOMES regulon activity drives NK cell maturation and cytotoxic programme; EOMES is required for terminal differentiation of CD56dim cytotoxic NK cells.
CD4 co-receptor expression defines helper T cell lineage; CD4 high expression is the canonical marker distinguishing CD4 from CD8 T cells.
CD4 and CD3E co-expression defines mature CD4 T cells; CD3E is the TCR-associated signalling subunit required for T cell identity, and CD4 specifies helper lineage.
CD8A co-receptor expression defines cytotoxic T cell lineage; CD8A high expression distinguishes CD8 from CD4 T cells.
CD8A and CD3E co-expression defines mature cytotoxic T cells; CD3E is required for TCR signalling and CD8A specifies the cytotoxic lineage.
SIGLEC1 (CD169/Sialoadhesin) is a high-confidence positive marker for plasmacytoid dendritic cells, particularly enriched in thymic pDCs.
IRF7 is the master transcription factor for pDC identity and type I IFN production; active IRF7 regulon drives the pDC-specific transcriptional programme including PDCA-1, BST2, and IFN-alpha genes.

Phase 1 correction: original rule checked IGKC absence (wrong — pDCs naturally express IGKC due to developmental B-lineage relationship, Rodrigues et al. 2018). Corrected rule: active PAX5 regulon (z >= 1.5) indicates mature B-cell identity and contradicts pDC. PAX5 drives B-cell-specific transcription; it is inactive in pDCs despite their B-lineage developmental origins.
IRF8 is the master transcription factor for cDC1 specification; IRF8 is required for BATF3-dependent cDC1 development and cross-presentation function.
BATF3 regulon activity is required for cDC1 lineage commitment and XCR1+ cross-presenting DC identity; BATF3 drives the type 1 conventional DC programme.
High SIGLEC1 (CD169) expression is specific to pDCs and macrophages; high SIGLEC1 in a putative cDC1 cluster indicates pDC contamination or misidentification.
CD1C (CD1c) is a canonical marker for cDC2 (CLEC10A+ type 2 conventional DC); high CD1C expression distinguishes cDC2 from cDC1 and pDC subsets.
IRF4 regulon activity drives cDC2 lineage specification; IRF4 is required for ESAM+ cDC2 development and distinguishes cDC2 from the IRF8-driven cDC1 lineage.
CD14 is the canonical surface marker for classical monocytes; high CD14 expression distinguishes classical monocytes from non-classical monocytes and macrophages.
SPI1 (PU.1) regulon activity is required for monocyte and myeloid identity; SPI1 drives the myeloid transcriptional programme including ITGAM, CD68, and cytokine receptor genes.
High SIGLEC1 is specific to pDCs and macrophages; classical monocytes express low SIGLEC1. High SIGLEC1 in a putative monocyte cluster indicates macrophage or pDC identity.
MRC1 (CD206, Mannose Receptor) is a canonical marker for tissue-resident macrophages; high MRC1 expression indicates alternatively-activated or tissue-resident macrophage identity.
SPI1 (PU.1) regulon activity is required for macrophage identity and myeloid differentiation; SPI1 co-ordinates expression of pattern recognition receptors and phagocytic machinery.
PAX5 is the master transcription factor for B-cell identity; active PAX5 regulon drives B-cell-specific gene expression including CD19, CD20, and immunoglobulin locus accessibility.
CD19 is the canonical B-cell surface marker expressed from pro-B through memory B cell stages; high CD19 expression strongly supports B-cell identity.
Co-expression of CD19 and CD20 (MS4A1) is the canonical signature of mature naive B cells; both are required for optimal BCR signalling complex assembly.
PRDM1 (BLIMP1) is the master regulator of plasma cell differentiation; active PRDM1 regulon drives immunoglobulin secretion programme and represses B-cell identity genes including PAX5.
XBP1 regulon activity drives the unfolded protein response required for high-rate immunoglobulin secretion in plasma cells; XBP1 is essential for ER expansion in antibody-secreting cells.

AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) active regulon is the defining feature of mature medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTEC-hi); AIRE drives promiscuous peripheral tissue antigen expression for central tolerance induction.
PSMB11 (beta5t) is exclusively expressed in cortical thymic epithelial cells and a subset of mTECs; high PSMB11 in mTEC context indicates mature thymic epithelial identity.
PSMB11 (beta5t) is the canonical cortical thymic epithelial cell marker; its expression in cTECs enables positive selection of CD4 and CD8 T cells.
IKZF2 (Helios) regulon is active in cTECs and drives the cortical thymic epithelial transcriptional programme required for positive selection of developing thymocytes.
NKT cells express an invariant TCR and thus carry TRAC (TCR alpha constant) expression; TRAC presence combined with NK markers distinguishes NKT from conventional NK cells.
TBX21 (T-bet) is active in NKT1 cells and drives IFN-gamma production; NKT cells share TBX21-driven effector programmes with NK cells and ILC1s.
Co-expression of CD3E (TCR signalling component) and KLRB1 (CD161, NKR-P1) is the canonical NKT signature; CD3E indicates T-cell receptor complex while CD161 marks NK-lineage commitment.
S100A8 (Calprotectin) is highly expressed in neutrophils and is a canonical neutrophil marker; S100A8/S100A9 heterodimer is released during neutrophil activation.
CEBPA regulon activity drives granulopoiesis and neutrophil differentiation; CEBPA is required for commitment to the neutrophil lineage from common myeloid progenitors.
CTLA4 (CD152) is constitutively expressed at high levels on Tregs; FOXP3 directly transactivates the CTLA4 locus and CTLA4-mediated co-stimulation blockade is a key Treg suppression mechanism.
IKZF2 (Helios) marks thymus-derived natural Tregs (nTregs); Helios high expression distinguishes nTregs from peripherally-induced iTregs and confirms thymic Treg origin.
IL-17A production is incompatible with Treg identity; FOXP3 and RORC are mutually exclusive master TFs. Th17/Treg plasticity exists but high IL17A contradicts stable FOXP3+ Treg fate.
Active RORC regulon is mutually exclusive with Treg identity; RORC-driven Th17 programming and FOXP3-driven Treg programming are reciprocally antagonistic transcriptional programmes.
CD3E is the TCR signalling subunit required for T-cell identity; high CD3E distinguishes T cells from NK cells and ILCs.
CD4 and CD8 co-receptors are mutually exclusive in mature T cells; high CD8A definitively excludes CD4+ T helper identity.
TRDC (TCR delta constant) expression marks gamma-delta T cells; high TRDC is incompatible with conventional CD4+ alpha-beta T-cell identity.
CD3E is required for TCR-complex signalling and T-cell identity; high CD3E co-expression with CD8A confirms cytotoxic T-cell lineage.
Granzyme B (GZMB) is a key effector cytotoxic molecule in CD8+ T cells; high GZMB marks cytotoxic effector CD8 T cells and supports cytotoxic lineage identity.
Perforin (PRF1) is essential for cytotoxic killing by CD8+ T cells; high PRF1 expression marks effector CD8 T cells and distinguishes them from helper T-cell subsets.
CD4 and CD8 expression are mutually exclusive in mature T cells; high CD4 definitively excludes cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell identity.
NKT cells express an invariant alpha-beta TCR (TRAV10/TRAJ18 in humans); high TRDC (gamma-delta TCR constant) is incompatible with NKT identity.
NKT cells express a TCR and require CD3E for TCR-complex signalling; high CD3E combined with NK markers (KLRB1) is the canonical NKT signature.
TBX21 (T-bet) is the master transcription factor for Th1 differentiation; TBX21 drives IFNG expression, IL-12 receptor upregulation, and CXCR3 expression required for Th1 effector function.
IFN-gamma (IFNG) is the canonical Th1 effector cytokine; high IFNG expression is directly driven by TBX21 and is the defining functional marker of Th1 cells.
CXCR3 is selectively expressed on Th1 cells and mediates their migration to inflammatory sites; CXCR3 upregulation is directly driven by TBX21 in Th1 polarised cells.
Active GATA3 regulon is mutually exclusive with Th1 identity; TBX21 directly represses GATA3 and vice versa in a bistable transcriptional switch controlling Th1/Th2 lineage commitment.
Active RORC regulon is incompatible with Th1 identity; TBX21 and RORC are mutually antagonistic master transcription factors controlling Th1/Th17 cell fate decisions.
Co-expression of IFNG and CXCR3 constitutes the canonical Th1 effector circuit; both are directly driven by TBX21 and together define the migratory and effector properties of Th1 cells.
GATA3 is the master transcription factor for Th2 differentiation; GATA3 drives IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 expression and is required for Th2 cell maintenance and allergic immune responses.
IL-13 is a canonical Th2 effector cytokine; high IL13 expression is driven by GATA3 and marks Th2 identity in inflammatory and allergic contexts.
CCR4 is selectively expressed on Th2 cells and mediates chemotaxis to CCL17/CCL22 gradients at allergic inflammatory sites; CCR4 is a reliable surface marker for Th2 identity.
Active TBX21 regulon is mutually exclusive with Th2 identity; TBX21 directly represses GATA3 transcription and vice versa, enforcing Th1/Th2 lineage exclusivity.
Active RORC regulon is incompatible with Th2 identity; GATA3 and RORC drive mutually exclusive transcriptional programmes (Th2 vs Th17).
Co-expression of IL13 and CCR4 is the canonical Th2 effector circuit; both are GATA3 target genes and together define the cytokine output and migratory properties of Th2 cells.

RORC (RORgammat) is the master transcription factor for Th17 differentiation; RORC drives IL-17A, IL-17F, IL-21, and IL-22 expression required for anti-fungal and anti-extracellular-bacterial immunity.
IL-17A is the canonical Th17 effector cytokine; high IL17A expression is directly controlled by RORC and marks Th17 identity in inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, and anti-fungal immunity.
Th17 cells are conventional alpha-beta T cells requiring TCR signalling; TRAC (TCR alpha constant) presence distinguishes Th17 from ILC3 (which also expresses RORC but lacks VDJ recombination).
CCR6 is selectively expressed on Th17 cells and is a downstream target of RORC; CCR6 mediates Th17 migration to mucosal surfaces and is a reliable surface marker for Th17 identity.
Active FOXP3 regulon is mutually exclusive with Th17 identity; FOXP3 directly represses RORC and IL-17A transcription. Th17/Treg plasticity exists but stable Th17 identity requires FOXP3 suppression.
Active TBX21 regulon is incompatible with Th17 identity; TBX21 suppresses RORC transcription and drives cells toward Th1 rather than Th17 fate.
Co-expression of IL17A cytokine and TRAC (TCR alpha) is the canonical Th17 distinguishing circuit; IL17A confirms RORC-driven Th17 programme while TRAC confirms T-cell (not ILC3) identity.
BCL6 is the master transcription factor for Tfh differentiation; BCL6 drives CXCR5 and PDCD1 expression required for germinal centre entry and B-cell help.
CXCR5 is the defining surface marker of Tfh cells; CXCR5 expression drives Tfh migration into B-cell follicles and germinal centres and is directly activated by BCL6.
PD-1 (PDCD1) is highly expressed on Tfh cells and is required for their interaction with PD-L1-expressing germinal centre B cells; high PDCD1 in CXCR5+ T cells confirms Tfh identity.
Active PRDM1 (BLIMP1) regulon is directly antagonistic to BCL6-driven Tfh identity; PRDM1 represses BCL6 and drives terminal effector differentiation, directly competing with Tfh fate.
Co-expression of CXCR5 and PD-1 (PDCD1) is the canonical surface marker circuit for Tfh cells; both are BCL6 target genes and their co-expression defines functional Tfh identity.

TOX is the master regulator of T-cell exhaustion; active TOX regulon drives epigenetic remodelling and transcriptional programmes of terminal exhaustion including PDCD1, HAVCR2, and LAG3 co-inhibitory receptor expression.
PD-1 (PDCD1) is the canonical co-inhibitory receptor of exhausted T cells; sustained high PDCD1 expression indicates chronic antigen exposure and progressive T-cell dysfunction.
TIM-3 (HAVCR2) co-expression with PD-1 marks terminally exhausted T cells; HAVCR2 upregulation correlates with loss of cytokine polyfunctionality in chronic viral infection and tumours.
LAG3 is a co-inhibitory receptor upregulated in exhausted T cells alongside PD-1 and TIM-3; high LAG3 marks progressive exhaustion and is a therapeutic target in tumour immunity.

Active TCF7 regulon marks progenitor-exhausted or stem-like memory T cells, not terminally exhausted Tex; TCF7 and TOX define the progenitor-exhausted vs terminally-exhausted axis and are mutually exclusive in deep exhaustion.

Co-expression of PD-1, TIM-3, and LAG3 is the canonical triple-inhibitory-receptor circuit defining terminally exhausted T cells; all three are driven by TOX and together define the maximal exhaustion phenotype.
TCF7 (TCF1) is the master regulator of central memory T-cell identity; active TCF7 regulon drives self-renewal capacity, CCR7 expression, and lymph-node homing required for central memory T cells.
CCR7 is the key lymph-node homing receptor defining central memory T cells; high CCR7 allows Tcm cells to recirculate through secondary lymphoid organs and access naive T-cell niches.
CD27 is highly expressed on central memory T cells and is downregulated during terminal effector differentiation; high CD27 combined with CCR7 defines the Tcm phenotype.
High TIM-3 (HAVCR2) expression marks exhausted T cells, not central memory cells; TIM-3 upregulation is incompatible with the self-renewal and lymph-node homing programme of Tcm cells.
Active TOX regulon drives epigenetic remodelling towards exhaustion; TOX activity is incompatible with the TCF7-driven self-renewal programme of central memory T cells.

Co-expression of CCR7 and CD27 is the canonical central memory T-cell surface circuit; both are TCF7-driven and together define the lymph-node homing and co-stimulatory self-renewal programme of Tcm cells.
Granzyme B (GZMB) is highly expressed in effector memory T cells and marks their cytotoxic potential; high GZMB combined with lack of CCR7 defines the Tem phenotype.

CX3CR1 is highly expressed on effector memory T cells and marks terminally differentiated effector-memory cells; CX3CR1hi T cells represent a distinct population with reduced lymph-node trafficking and enhanced peripheral tissue patrol.
Granzyme K (GZMK) is expressed in circulating effector memory T cells at an earlier differentiation stage than GZMB; GZMK+GZMB co-expression marks terminally differentiated Tem cells.
High CCR7 expression is restricted to naive and central memory T cells; effector memory T cells downregulate CCR7 and lack lymph-node homing capacity, defining the Tcm/Tem distinction.

Co-expression of GZMB and GZMK defines terminally differentiated effector memory T cells; this granzyme co-expression circuit distinguishes Tem from early effector cells and reflects a distinct epigenetic state of cytotoxic licensing.
SLC4A10 is the most specific transcriptomic marker for MAIT cells in humans; high SLC4A10 expression reliably identifies MAIT cells across tissues and distinguishes them from other T-cell subsets.

CD161 (KLRB1) is constitutively expressed at high levels on MAIT cells and is a key surface marker; CD161 combined with SLC4A10 provides a robust transcriptomic signature for MAIT cell identification.
Active BCL6 regulon is incompatible with MAIT cell identity; MAIT cells do not enter germinal centres and are not Tfh cells; BCL6 activity is restricted to Tfh lineage among T-cell subsets.

Co-expression of SLC4A10 and CD161 (KLRB1) is the canonical MAIT cell transcriptomic circuit; both are driven by the MAIT-specific transcriptional programme and together provide high-confidence MAIT cell identification in scRNA-seq data.

TRDC (TCR delta constant region) is the definitive molecular marker of gamma-delta T cells; high TRDC expression unambiguously identifies gd T cells and distinguishes them from alpha-beta T cells (which express TRAC/TRBC).
TRGC1 (TCR gamma constant 1) encodes the gamma chain of the gd TCR; high TRGC1 combined with TRDC confirms gd T-cell identity and their non-classical T-cell lineage.
TRAC (TCR alpha constant) is expressed only in alpha-beta T cells; gd T cells express gamma-delta TCR chains (TRGC1/TRDC) and not TRAC. TRAC presence definitively contradicts gd T-cell identity.

Co-expression of TRDC (TCR delta constant) and TRGC1 (TCR gamma constant 1) is the canonical gd T-cell circuit; both chains must be co-expressed to form a functional gd TCR complex, providing high-specificity identification.
TRAC (TCR alpha constant) expression is exclusive to T cells; TRAC presence in a B-cell candidate contradicts B-cell identity and indicates a T cell or NKT cell contamination.
MS4A1 (CD20) is a canonical B-cell surface marker expressed on mature naive and memory B cells; CD20 is a target of anti-CD20 therapeutic antibodies and reliably marks mature B-cell identity.
SDC1 (CD138/Syndecan-1) is the canonical plasma cell surface marker; high SDC1 expression marks terminally differentiated antibody-secreting plasma cells and distinguishes them from plasmablasts.

Active PAX5 regulon is incompatible with plasma cell identity; PRDM1/BLIMP1 directly represses PAX5 during plasma cell differentiation, and residual PAX5 activity contradicts terminal plasma cell fate.

EBF1 (Early B-cell Factor 1) is the earliest committed B-lineage transcription factor; active EBF1 regulon drives commitment to B-cell fate from common lymphoid progenitors by activating Pax5 and V(D)J recombination machinery.
CD34 is expressed on early haematopoietic progenitors including pro-B cells; high CD34 combined with EBF1 and PAX5 marks the earliest B-cell-committed progenitor stage.

PAX5 is the master regulator of B-cell lineage commitment; active PAX5 regulon at the pro-B stage drives expression of B-cell-specific surface proteins and commits progenitors irreversibly to B-cell fate.

Co-activity of EBF1 and PAX5 regulons defines the pro-B cell transcriptional programme; EBF1 activates PAX5 which in turn stabilises B-cell commitment, forming a positive feedback loop required for B lymphopoiesis.

VPREB1 (VpreB1) is a component of the surrogate light chain expressed specifically at the pre-B cell stage; high VPREB1 combined with IGLL1 forms the pre-BCR complex required for pre-B cell selection and proliferation.

IGLL1 (lambda5 surrogate light chain) is co-expressed with VPREB1 at the pre-B cell stage to form the pre-BCR; high IGLL1 marks the large cycling pre-B cell population undergoing immunoglobulin light chain rearrangement.
PAX5 remains actively expressed throughout pre-B cell development, maintaining B-cell identity and driving expression of pre-BCR signalling components.
High IGHD (IgD) expression is restricted to mature naive B cells that have completed V(D)J recombination; IGHD expression in a pre-B cell candidate contradicts the pre-B developmental stage.

IGHD (IgD heavy chain constant region) co-expression with IgM is the canonical naive B cell phenotype; high IGHD marks B cells that have completed V(D)J recombination but have not undergone somatic hypermutation or class switching.
High IgM (IGHM) co-expression with IgD defines the naive B cell surface phenotype; naive B cells are IgM+IgD+ and transition to IgD-low after antigen activation.

TCL1A is highly expressed in naive and transitional B cells and is a reliable transcriptomic marker for naive B cell identification in scRNA-seq; TCL1A expression declines upon B cell activation and memory formation.
High CD27 expression marks antigen-experienced memory B cells; CD27 high in a putative naive B cell cluster indicates memory B cells, contradicting naive B cell identity.

Co-expression of IGHD and IGHM is the canonical naive B cell isotype circuit; both chains are co-expressed on the surface of naive B cells before antigen encounter and are both downregulated upon activation and class switching.
CD27 is the canonical memory B cell surface marker; high CD27 expression marks antigen-experienced B cells that have undergone germinal centre reactions and somatic hypermutation.

AICDA (AID/Activation-Induced Cytidine Deaminase) activity marks B cells undergoing or having recently undergone somatic hypermutation; AICDA expression is a reliable marker for germinal centre-experienced memory B cells.

High IGHD expression marks naive B cells; in memory B cells, IGHD is downregulated following activation and class switching. High IGHD in a memory B cell candidate contradicts antigen-experienced identity.
IGLL1 (surrogate light chain) is restricted to the pre-B cell stage; high IGLL1 in a memory B cell candidate indicates contamination with immature B cell precursors.

Co-expression of CD27 and CD38 (at intermediate levels) defines a transitional memory B cell or recently activated memory B cell population; both markers together distinguish memory B cells from naive (CD27-) and plasma cells (CD38hi SDC1hi).

AICDA (AID) is the enzyme catalysing somatic hypermutation and class-switch recombination; high AICDA expression is the definitive molecular marker of germinal centre B cells undergoing affinity maturation.

BCL6 is the master transcription factor of germinal centre B cells; active BCL6 regulon drives the GC B cell programme including AICDA expression, Tfh interaction, and suppression of premature plasma cell differentiation via PRDM1 repression.
CXCR4 is highly expressed on dark-zone germinal centre B cells (centroblasts); CXCR4 mediates migration to the dark zone where rapid proliferation and somatic hypermutation occur.
FAS (CD95/TNFRSF6) is highly expressed on germinal centre B cells and mediates selection-induced apoptosis of low-affinity clones; high FAS marks GC B cells undergoing affinity maturation selection.

Co-expression of AICDA and CXCR4 is the canonical dark-zone germinal centre B cell circuit; AICDA drives somatic hypermutation while CXCR4 positions centroblasts in the dark zone for rapid proliferation.
PRDM1 (BLIMP1) is the master regulator of plasma cell differentiation; active PRDM1 regulon drives plasmablast commitment and immunoglobulin secretion while repressing B-cell identity genes.
High CD38 expression marks plasmablasts and plasma cells at all stages of antibody-secreting cell differentiation; CD38 high combined with CD27 and active PRDM1 defines the plasmablast state.

High SDC1 (CD138) expression marks terminally differentiated plasma cells that have home to the bone marrow; plasmablasts express lower SDC1 than mature plasma cells, distinguishing them from fully differentiated antibody-secreting cells.
Co-expression of CD38 and CD27 at high levels defines the plasmablast circuit; both markers are upregulated upon B-cell activation and differentiation toward the antibody-secreting cell lineage.
FCGR3A (CD16a) is expressed on mature NK cells and mediates antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC); high FCGR3A distinguishes cytotoxic CD56dim NK cells from CD56bright NK cells.
NKG7 (Natural Killer Cell Granule Protein 7) is highly expressed in NK cells and cytotoxic lymphocytes; high NKG7 marks NK cell identity and cytotoxic potential.
KLRC1 (NKG2A/CD94) is a key inhibitory NK cell receptor; high KLRC1 marks mature NK cells and is involved in self-tolerance through recognition of HLA-E.
NCR1 (NKp46) is a natural cytotoxicity receptor expressed on virtually all NK cells; high NCR1 is a pan-NK marker and mediates recognition of stressed/virus-infected target cells.
High KLRB1 (CD161/NKR-P1) combined with TCR marks NKT cells rather than conventional NK cells; high KLRB1 alone is not specific but combined with NK cell context may indicate NKT contamination.
NCR1 (NKp46) is expressed on liver-resident ILC1 cells and distinguishes them from conventional NK cells; ILC1 co-expresses NKp46 with TBX21 and IFNG but lacks EOMES and perforin.
IFN-gamma (IFNG) is the primary effector cytokine of ILC1 cells; high IFNG is driven by TBX21 in ILC1 and is their key functional readout distinguishing them from ILC2 and ILC3.
Active EOMES regulon marks conventional NK cells rather than ILC1; ILC1 are EOMES-negative which distinguishes them from mature NK cells that require EOMES for terminal differentiation.
High perforin (PRF1) expression marks cytotoxic NK cells; ILC1 cells are non-cytotoxic and PRF1-negative, distinguishing them from NK cells in the same tissue compartment.
IL-4 is the canonical ILC2 effector cytokine driving type 2 immune responses; high IL4 expression is directly activated by GATA3 in ILC2 cells.
IL1RL1 (ST2/IL-33R) is the canonical ILC2 surface marker; high IL1RL1 marks IL-33-responsive ILC2 cells in lung, gut, and other barrier tissues.
PTGDR2 (CRTH2/CD294) is a prostaglandin D2 receptor selectively expressed on ILC2 cells; high PTGDR2 is a reliable surface marker that distinguishes ILC2 from ILC1 and ILC3.
Active TBX21 regulon is incompatible with ILC2 identity; TBX21 and GATA3 are mutually antagonistic master TFs driving ILC1/NK (TBX21) versus ILC2 (GATA3) fate.

Co-expression of ST2 (IL1RL1) and CRTH2 (PTGDR2) is the canonical ILC2 surface circuit; both are GATA3-driven and together enable ILC2 response to alarmin signals (IL-33 and PGD2) at barrier surfaces.
IL-22 is the primary effector cytokine of ILC3 cells at mucosal surfaces; high IL22 is directly driven by RORC and is the key functional output of ILC3, mediating anti-microbial barrier defence.
LTB (Lymphotoxin-beta) is expressed by ILC3 and is required for lymphoid tissue organogenesis; high LTB marks tissue-forming ILC3 populations and their role in tertiary lymphoid structure formation.

Co-expression of IL22 and LTB defines the effector ILC3 programme; both are RORC-driven and together capture the cytokine output and tissue-organising functions of intestinal and lymphoid-tissue ILC3.

CCR6 is expressed on ILC3 cells and mediates their positioning at mucosal surfaces; CCR6 distinguishes NCR-negative ILC3 from NCR-positive ILC3 and is a reliable marker for the lymphoid-tissue inducer ILC3 subset.
IFN-gamma production is a key effector function of NKT1 cells; high IFNG combined with TRAC and KLRB1 confirms NKT identity and distinguishes NKT1 from NKT2/NKT17 subsets.
NKT cells express an invariant alpha-beta TCR; high TRDC (TCR delta constant, marking gamma-delta T cells) is incompatible with NKT identity.
SLC4A10 is the most specific marker of MAIT cells; high SLC4A10 in an NKT candidate indicates MAIT cell identity rather than NKT, as both share CD161 expression but differ in TCR usage.
High FCGR3A (CD16a) expression is the defining marker of CD56dim cytotoxic NK cells; CD56dim NK cells mediate ADCC and direct cytotoxicity and constitute ~90% of peripheral blood NK cells.
Granzyme B is highly expressed in CD56dim NK cells and mediates their cytotoxic killing; high GZMB combined with high CD16/FCGR3A defines the terminally differentiated cytotoxic NK cell phenotype.
Perforin (PRF1) is constitutively expressed in CD56dim NK cells at high levels; PRF1 mediates granule-mediated cytotoxicity and is a reliable marker for the cytotoxic NK cell subset.
CD56dim NK cells lack CCR7 expression and do not traffic to lymph nodes; high CCR7 in a CD56dim NK candidate indicates a CD56bright NK cell or T cell rather than a classical cytotoxic NK cell.
Co-expression of CD16 (FCGR3A) and Granzyme B (GZMB) is the canonical CD56dim cytotoxic NK cell circuit; both are required for the full cytotoxic potential of peripheral blood NK cells.

Very high NCAM1 (CD56) expression is the defining feature of CD56bright NK cells; CD56bright NK cells are the regulatory subset that produces immunomodulatory cytokines rather than mediating direct cytotoxicity.
XCL1 (lymphotactin) is selectively expressed by CD56bright NK cells and recruits BATF3+ cDC1 cells; high XCL1 combined with low CD16 defines the cytokine-producing NK cell subset.
CCR7 is expressed on CD56bright NK cells and enables their trafficking to lymph nodes; high CCR7 distinguishes regulatory CD56bright NK from cytotoxic CD56dim NK cells.
High FCGR3A (CD16) expression marks cytotoxic CD56dim NK cells; CD56bright NK cells express low to absent CD16, and high FCGR3A contradicts CD56bright identity.

Co-expression of XCL1 and high NCAM1 (CD56) is the canonical CD56bright NK cell circuit; XCL1 mediates DC recruitment while high CD56 marks the regulatory NK subset, together defining the immunomodulatory NK cell identity.
IL7R (CD127) is highly expressed on ILC progenitors (ILCP) and all mature ILC subsets; high IL7R combined with ID2 marks the ILC lineage progenitor before subset commitment.

ID2 is a transcriptional repressor required for ILC lineage specification; high ID2 expression marks common ILC progenitors committed to the ILC fate but before Th1/Th2/Th3-like subset differentiation.
ILC progenitors develop without VDJ recombination; TRAC presence indicates a committed T-cell progenitor (ITP) rather than an ILC progenitor.

Co-expression of IL7R and ID2 is the canonical ILC progenitor circuit; IL7R provides survival and proliferation signals while ID2 enforces ILC fate commitment by repressing T-cell and B-cell programmes.
Adaptive NK cells are mature cytotoxic NK cells that have expanded in response to HCMV; high FCGR3A (CD16) is retained on adaptive NK cells and mediates enhanced ADCC.

KLRC2 (NKG2C) is the defining surface marker of adaptive NK cells; high NKG2C expression specifically marks the HCMV-expanded adaptive NK cell population that persists long-term after viral infection.

High KLRC1 (NKG2A) marks conventional NK cells; adaptive NKG2C+ NK cells are predominantly NKG2A-negative due to epigenetic silencing, and high KLRC1 in an adaptive NK candidate contradicts NKG2C+ adaptive NK identity.
Adaptive NK cells exhibit reduced EOMES expression compared to conventional NK cells; high EOMES activity is more consistent with conventional NK cell identity.
Co-expression of NKG2C (KLRC2) and CD16 (FCGR3A) is the canonical adaptive NK cell circuit; NKG2C identifies HCMV-expanded NK cells while CD16 enables their enhanced ADCC function.
FCGR1 (CD64/FcgammaRI) is a high-affinity IgG Fc receptor expressed on classical monocytes; high CD64 marks activated monocytes and distinguishes them from patrolling non-classical monocytes.
S100A9 is constitutively expressed at high levels in monocytes and is the S100A8/S100A9 calprotectin complex component; high S100A9 combined with CD14 reliably marks classical monocyte identity.
LST1 is a leukocyte-specific transcript expressed on monocytes and neutrophils; high LST1 marks myeloid cell identity and is useful for distinguishing monocytes from lymphoid cells.
AIF1 (IBA1/Ionised calcium-binding Adaptor molecule 1) is a pan-macrophage/microglia marker; high AIF1 expression reliably marks tissue-resident macrophages across all tissue types.

TREM2 is expressed on tissue-resident macrophages in homeostatic states; high TREM2 marks tissue-resident macrophages in liver (Kupffer cells), brain (microglia), and adipose tissue, distinguishing them from monocyte-derived inflammatory macrophages.
High S100B expression marks neural/glial cells rather than macrophages; S100B high in a macrophage candidate indicates astrocytes or neural progenitors contaminating the macrophage cluster.
XCR1 (Chemokine CXC Receptor 1) is the most specific surface marker for cDC1 cells; high XCR1 expression marks cross-presenting cDC1 cells that produce XCL1-attracting NK cells and CD8 T cells.
CLEC9A (DNGR-1) is a dead cell-sensing C-type lectin exclusively expressed by cDC1 cells; high CLEC9A is the most selective cDC1 marker and drives cross-presentation of cell-associated antigens.
CLEC10A (CD301/MGL) is a C-type lectin selectively expressed by cDC2 cells; high CLEC10A marks the type 2 conventional DC subset and distinguishes cDC2 from cDC1 and pDC.
XCR1 expression is strictly restricted to cDC1 cells; XCR1 high in a cDC2 candidate indicates cDC1 contamination or misidentification.
BST2 (CD317/Tetherin) is constitutively expressed on pDC cells and is induced by IFN-alpha; high BST2 is a reliable pDC surface marker and is upregulated during the pDC type I IFN response.
TCF4 (E2-2) is the master transcription factor for pDC specification; active TCF4 regulon drives pDC-specific gene expression including SIGLEC1, BST2, and type I IFN genes.
MPO (Myeloperoxidase) is a neutrophil-specific enzyme stored in primary azurophilic granules; high MPO expression is a definitive marker of neutrophil identity and cytotoxic oxidative burst capacity.
CXCR2 is the primary IL-8 receptor mediating neutrophil chemotaxis; high CXCR2 expression marks mature neutrophils and is required for their recruitment to inflammatory sites.
S100A9 is highly expressed in neutrophils as part of the S100A8/A9 calprotectin complex; high S100A9 combined with MPO and CXCR2 defines neutrophil identity.
High FCGR3A (CD16) combined with low CD14 defines the non-classical patrolling monocyte; CD16hi CD14lo monocytes patrol vessel walls and are the first responders to viral infections.
CX3CR1 (fractalkine receptor) is highly expressed on non-classical patrolling monocytes; high CX3CR1 drives their adherence to and patrol of blood vessel endothelium.
High CD14 marks classical monocytes; non-classical monocytes are CD14lo CD16hi, and high CD14 in a non-classical monocyte candidate contradicts patrolling monocyte identity.
Co-expression of CD16 (FCGR3A) and CX3CR1 is the canonical non-classical patrolling monocyte circuit; together they enable vessel-wall surveillance and antiviral immune patrol.
CXCL9 (MIG) is a classical activation marker produced by M1 macrophages in response to IFN-gamma; high CXCL9 marks the pro-inflammatory classically-activated macrophage state.
CXCL10 (IP-10) is co-expressed with CXCL9 in IFN-gamma-activated M1 macrophages; high CXCL10 is a canonical marker of classically activated macrophages and drives Th1 T cell recruitment.

IDO1 (Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase 1) is an IFN-gamma-induced enzyme highly expressed in M1 macrophages; high IDO1 marks pro-inflammatory macrophages mediating T cell suppression through tryptophan depletion.
High MRC1 (CD206/Mannose Receptor) marks alternatively activated M2 macrophages; MRC1 expression is suppressed by the M1 polarisation programme and its high expression contradicts M1 identity.

Co-expression of CXCL9 and CXCL10 is the canonical M1 macrophage chemokine circuit; both are driven by IFN-gamma/STAT1 signalling and together recruit Th1 cells and cytotoxic lymphocytes to inflammatory foci.

MRC1 (CD206/Mannose Receptor) is the canonical alternatively activated M2 macrophage marker; high MRC1 marks IL-4/IL-13-polarised macrophages mediating tissue repair, parasite killing, and tumour promotion.
CD163 is a haemoglobin scavenger receptor expressed at high levels on alternatively activated M2 macrophages; high CD163 marks anti-inflammatory macrophages and is a reliable M2 surface marker.

High IDO1 marks pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages activated by IFN-gamma; IDO1 expression is suppressed in M2-polarised macrophages, and its high expression contradicts M2/alternative activation identity.
CXCL9 is an IFN-gamma-driven M1 chemokine; high CXCL9 marks classically activated macrophages and contradicts M2/anti-inflammatory macrophage identity.

Co-expression of MRC1 (CD206) and CD163 is the canonical M2 alternatively activated macrophage circuit; both are driven by IL-4/IL-13 signalling and together define the tissue-remodelling anti-inflammatory macrophage state.

PPARG is the master regulator of alveolar macrophage identity; active PPARG regulon is required for alveolar macrophage self-maintenance and drives expression of FABP4 and surfactant catabolism genes.

FABP4 (Fatty Acid Binding Protein 4) is a highly specific marker for alveolar macrophages; high FABP4 is directly driven by PPARG and marks the lipid-metabolising phenotype of lung-resident macrophages.

MARCO (Macrophage Receptor with Collagenous Structure) is a class A scavenger receptor expressed at high levels on alveolar macrophages; high MARCO marks tissue-resident lung macrophages and their phagocytic programme.

Co-expression of FABP4 and MARCO is the canonical alveolar macrophage circuit; FABP4 marks the lipid-metabolising programme while MARCO marks the phagocytic programme, together defining lung-resident macrophage identity.

KIT (CD117/c-Kit) is the canonical mast cell receptor; high KIT expression marks mast cells across all tissue compartments and is required for mast cell development, survival, and activation via SCF/KITLG.

TPSAB1 (tryptase alpha/beta 1) is a mast cell-specific serine protease stored in secretory granules; high TPSAB1 is the most specific transcriptomic marker for mast cells and is released during mast cell degranulation.

CPA3 (Carboxypeptidase A3) is a mast cell-specific exopeptidase co-stored with tryptase in secretory granules; high CPA3 combined with TPSAB1 and KIT provides high-confidence mast cell identification.

Co-expression of KIT (CD117) and TPSAB1 (tryptase) is the canonical mast cell circuit; KIT drives mast cell survival and activation while TPSAB1 is the definitive functional marker of mast cell granule content.

SIGLEC8 is an inhibitory receptor expressed exclusively on eosinophils in the blood; high SIGLEC8 is the most specific transcriptomic marker for eosinophils and distinguishes them from other granulocytes.

CCR3 (eotaxin receptor) is highly expressed on eosinophils and mediates their recruitment to allergic inflammatory sites via eotaxin-1/2/3 gradients; high CCR3 is a reliable eosinophil surface marker.

Co-expression of SIGLEC8 and CCR3 is the canonical eosinophil identification circuit; SIGLEC8 provides high specificity while CCR3 confirms the allergic/type-2-immune-response context of eosinophil identity.
AGER (RAGE) is the canonical surface marker of AT1 cells, mediating innate immune sensing at the air-blood barrier and required for alveolar spreading.
PDPN (podoplanin/T1alpha) is highly expressed on AT1 cells and required for their flat morphology; marks the air-blood barrier epithelium.
SFTPC (surfactant protein C) is exclusively expressed by AT2 cells; its presence contradicts AT1 identity.
SFTPB (surfactant protein B) marks AT2 cells; high SFTPB contradicts flat AT1 epithelial identity.
Co-expression of AGER and PDPN defines the AT1 cell surface phenotype; both are required to confirm the flat air-blood barrier epithelial identity.
SFTPC (surfactant protein C) is the definitive AT2 marker; it is produced exclusively by AT2 cells and drives surfactant film formation in alveoli.
LAMP3 (CD63) marks the lamellar bodies of AT2 cells where surfactant is stored before secretion; highly AT2-specific in the lung.
AGER marks AT1 cells; high AGER expression contradicts the cuboidal AT2 identity with lamellar body surfactant production.
Co-expression of SFTPC and SFTPB (surfactant proteins C and B) is the definitive AT2 circuit; both are required for functional surfactant and lamellar body biogenesis.
SCGB1A1 (CC16/uteroglobin) is the primary secreted protein of Club cells; it is the defining marker of this non-ciliated secretory bronchiolar cell type.
CYP2B6 is the primary xenobiotic-metabolizing cytochrome P450 in the bronchiolar epithelium and is selectively enriched in Club cells for detoxification.
FOXJ1 is the master TF of ciliated cell differentiation; its activation contradicts Club cell identity since Club cells are non-ciliated secretory cells.
Co-expression of SCGB1A1 (secretory marker) and CYP2B6 (xenobiotic metabolism) confirms the secretory/detoxifying Club cell identity of bronchiolar epithelium.
FOXJ1 is the evolutionarily conserved master transcription factor of motile ciliogenesis, required for the transcriptional programme that assembles the axoneme.
DNAI1 (dynein axonemal intermediate chain 1) is a structural component of the outer dynein arm motor complex; its high expression marks motile ciliated airway cells.
SCGB1A1 marks Club cells; ciliated cells are a distinct non-secretory population and SCGB1A1 expression contradicts ciliated identity.
Co-expression of FOXJ1 (ciliogenesis master TF) and DNAI1 (dynein motor structural component) confirms motile ciliated cell identity; both are required for functional axoneme assembly.
TP63 (p63) is the master transcription factor for basal cell identity in the trachea and airway; it is required for basal cell self-renewal and progenitor maintenance.
KRT5 (keratin 5) is an intermediate filament structural marker of basal cells in pseudostratified airway epithelium, co-expressed with TP63.
SFTPC marks differentiated AT2 cells; basal progenitors do not express surfactant proteins, so SFTPC presence contradicts basal identity.
FOXJ1 activation drives ciliated differentiation; its activity is incompatible with the undifferentiated basal progenitor state defined by TP63.
Co-expression of TP63 (basal master TF) and KRT5 (basal structural keratin) is the canonical basal cell circuit in airway epithelium.
MUC5AC is the primary gel-forming mucin secreted by airway goblet cells; it forms the mucus gel layer protecting the bronchial epithelium.
MUC5B is the second gel-forming mucin co-expressed with MUC5AC in goblet cells; essential for mucociliary clearance in airways.
SCGB1A1 is the Club cell secreted protein; goblet and Club cells are distinct secretory populations and SCGB1A1 presence contradicts goblet identity.
Co-expression of MUC5AC and MUC5B defines the mucus-producing goblet cell secretory program in airway epithelium.
ALB (albumin) is the principal secretory protein of hepatocytes, constituting ~50% of plasma proteins; it is synthesized almost exclusively by hepatocytes.
SERPINA1 (alpha-1 antitrypsin) is produced almost exclusively by hepatocytes and is a major plasma protease inhibitor; high expression confirms hepatocyte identity.
PTPRC (CD45) is expressed on all leukocytes; high CD45 in a liver cluster contradicts hepatocyte identity and indicates immune cell contamination.
KRT19 (CK19) marks biliary epithelial/cholangiocyte lineage; high KRT19 in a presumed hepatocyte cluster indicates cholangiocyte or ductal identity.
Co-expression of ALB (albumin, protein synthesis) and APOC3 (apolipoprotein C-III, lipid secretion) confirms the dual anabolic metabolic identity of hepatocytes.
LYVE1 (lymphatic vessel hyaluronic acid receptor 1) is highly enriched in LSEC compared to other endothelial cells; it mediates hyaluronan scavenging from the blood.
CLEC4G (C-type lectin domain family 4 member G) is a pattern-recognition receptor highly specific for LSEC, mediating hepatic clearance of glycoproteins.
PECAM1 (CD31) is high on vascular endothelium but low/absent on LSEC; high CD31 contradicts LSEC identity and suggests portal or central vein endothelium.
Co-expression of LYVE1 and CLEC4G is specific to liver sinusoidal endothelial cells; together they confirm the scavenger endothelial identity unique to the hepatic sinusoid.
CLEC4F is a C-type lectin uniquely expressed by Kupffer cells among liver macrophages; it distinguishes resident Kupffer cells from monocyte-derived macrophages.
VSIG4 (CRIg, complement receptor of the Ig superfamily) is highly expressed on Kupffer cells for phagocytosis of complement-opsonized pathogens from the portal blood.
FCGR3A (CD16) marks monocyte-derived macrophages and patrolling monocytes; resident Kupffer cells are CD16-negative, and high CD16 contradicts Kupffer cell identity.
Co-expression of CLEC4F and VSIG4 is unique to resident Kupffer cells and distinguishes them from monocyte-derived hepatic macrophages that lack both markers.
LRAT (lecithin retinol acyltransferase) is highly expressed in quiescent hepatic stellate cells, which store 50-80% of the body's vitamin A in cytoplasmic lipid droplets.
PDGFRB (PDGF receptor beta) is expressed on hepatic stellate cells and mediates PDGF-driven proliferation and activation during fibrosis.
ALB is a hepatocyte-specific secretory protein; its high expression contradicts stellate cell identity and indicates parenchymal hepatocyte contamination.
Co-expression of LRAT (vitamin A storage) and PDGFRB (PDGF signaling) identifies hepatic stellate cells across quiescent and activated states, distinguishing them from portal fibroblasts.
KRT19 (cytokeratin 19/CK19) is the canonical biliary epithelial marker; it is selectively expressed in cholangiocytes lining intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts.
SOX9 is required for biliary specification and maintains ductal morphology; its regulon activity marks cholangiocytes and distinguishes them from hepatocytes.
ALB is expressed exclusively by hepatocytes; its high expression contradicts cholangiocyte identity, as biliary epithelial cells do not produce albumin.
Co-expression of KRT19 (biliary keratin) and EPCAM (epithelial cell adhesion molecule, marks ductal plate and bile duct) confirms cholangiocyte identity.
FABP1 (liver-type fatty acid binding protein) is highly expressed in small intestinal enterocytes for intracellular fatty acid transport from the brush border.
SI (sucrase-isomaltase) is a brush border hydrolase expressed exclusively by mature villous enterocytes for disaccharide digestion; its expression marks terminal enterocyte differentiation.
MUC2 is the goblet cell gel-forming mucin; its high expression contradicts absorptive enterocyte identity and indicates goblet cell lineage.
Co-expression of FABP1 (lipid transport) and SI (brush border hydrolase) marks mature absorptive villous enterocytes with full digestive and absorptive capacity.
SLC26A3 (DRA, downregulated in adenoma) is the primary Cl-/HCO3- exchanger of colonocytes, required for electrolyte absorption in the large intestine.
CA2 (carbonic anhydrase II) provides the bicarbonate for Cl-/HCO3- exchange in colonocytes and is highly expressed in colonic absorptive epithelium.
SI (sucrase-isomaltase) marks small intestinal villous enterocytes; its absence in colonocytes is a key regional distinction of large intestinal absorptive epithelium.
MUC2 marks goblet cells; high MUC2 expression contradicts absorptive colonocyte identity and indicates goblet cell lineage in the large intestine.
Co-expression of SLC26A3 (anion exchanger) and CA2 (bicarbonate source) defines the electrolyte-absorbing colonocyte program and distinguishes colonocytes from small intestinal enterocytes.
MUC2 is the major gel-forming mucin of the intestinal mucus layer; it is secreted exclusively by goblet cells and forms the protective mucus barrier over the epithelium.
TFF3 (trefoil factor 3/intestinal trefoil factor) is co-secreted with MUC2 by goblet cells to stabilize the mucus gel and promote mucosal healing.
FABP1 marks absorptive enterocytes; goblet cells are secretory and do not express high levels of lipid transport proteins, so FABP1 presence contradicts goblet identity.
Co-expression of MUC2 (mucin gel) and TFF3 (mucus stabilizer) defines the goblet cell mucus secretory program throughout the intestine.
DEFA5 (alpha-defensin 5) is secreted exclusively by Paneth cells in human ileum and provides innate antibacterial defense at the intestinal crypt base.
LYZ (lysozyme) is produced at high levels by Paneth cells and cleaves bacterial cell walls; it is co-secreted with defensins as part of the Paneth cell antimicrobial arsenal.
MUC2 marks mucus-secreting goblet cells; Paneth cells secrete antimicrobial peptides rather than mucins, so high MUC2 contradicts Paneth cell identity.
Co-expression of DEFA5 (defensin-5) and LYZ (lysozyme) constitutes the Paneth cell antimicrobial secretory circuit at the intestinal crypt base.
CHGA (chromogranin A) is a pan-enteroendocrine marker co-packaged with gut hormones in dense-core secretory vesicles; it is the canonical EEC diagnostic marker.
NEUROD1 is a bHLH transcription factor required for enteroendocrine cell fate specification; its regulon activity drives EEC differentiation from secretory progenitors.
FABP1 is an absorptive enterocyte marker; enteroendocrine cells are hormone-secreting and do not express lipid transport proteins, so high FABP1 contradicts EEC identity.
Co-expression of CHGA (secretory vesicle marker) and PCSK1 (prohormone convertase 1, required for active gut hormone processing) confirms enteroendocrine identity with active hormone secretion.
TRPM5 (transient receptor potential cation channel M5) drives the bitter/chemical taste-sensing cascade in intestinal tuft cells, linking luminal detection to type 2 immune signaling.
DCLK1 (doublecortin-like kinase 1) is required for the tuft cell morphological program including long apical microvilli; it is the principal morphological marker of tuft cells.
MUC2 marks mucus-secreting goblet cells; tuft cells are chemosensory and do not produce mucins, so high MUC2 contradicts tuft cell identity.
DEFA5 marks Paneth cells at the crypt base; tuft cells are a distinct chemosensory lineage scattered throughout villi and crypts and do not produce Paneth defensins.
Co-expression of TRPM5 (chemosensory signaling) and DCLK1 (tuft morphology) confirms intestinal tuft cell identity; this combination is not found in any other gut epithelial cell type.
VGLUT1 (SLC17A7) is the vesicular glutamate transporter expressed in cortical excitatory neurons. Its high expression is the defining marker of glutamatergic identity.
GAD1 encodes glutamate decarboxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme for GABA synthesis. Its presence defines inhibitory neurons and is mutually exclusive with glutamatergic identity.
GAD2 (GAD65) is a second glutamate decarboxylase isoform co-expressed with GAD1 in all inhibitory neurons. Its presence eliminates excitatory neuron identity.
CaMKII alpha (CAMK2A) is selectively expressed in excitatory pyramidal neurons and drives synaptic plasticity. High expression confirms glutamatergic identity.
Co-expression of GAD1 and GAD2 defines GABAergic interneurons. Both isoforms of glutamate decarboxylase are required together for robust GABA synthesis in inhibitory neurons.
VGLUT1 (SLC17A7) marks glutamatergic neurons and is mutually exclusive with GABAergic identity. Its presence rules out inhibitory neuron classification.
Somatostatin (SST) marks one of the major inhibitory interneuron subtypes (Martinotti cells). High SST expression supports inhibitory neuron identity.
Parvalbumin (PVALB) marks fast-spiking basket and chandelier interneurons. High expression is a key inhibitory neuron marker.
Homeostatic astrocytes co-express AQP4 (water channel), SLC1A2 (GLT-1 glutamate transporter), GJA1 (connexin 43 for gap junctions), and S100B. This quartet defines the homeostatic astrocyte program.
LCN2 (lipocalin-2) is an A1 reactive astrocyte marker induced by neuroinflammation. Its high expression marks reactive, not homeostatic, astrocytes.
ALDH1L1 (10-formyltetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase) is a pan-astrocyte marker enriched in homeostatic astrocytes and used to distinguish them from other glia.

A1 reactive astrocytes are characterized by strong upregulation of GFAP (structural), LCN2 (inflammatory), and C3 (complement). This triad is induced by activated microglia via IL-1alpha, TNF, and C1q.
GFAP is strongly upregulated in reactive astrocytes compared to homeostatic astrocytes. Very high GFAP is the hallmark of astrogliosis.
Mature oligodendrocytes co-express the major myelin proteins MBP, MAG, MOG, and PLP1. This quartet defines the myelinating oligodendrocyte program and is absent in OPCs.
PDGFRA marks oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) and is downregulated upon OPC differentiation into mature oligodendrocytes. PDGFRA presence excludes mature myelinating oligodendrocyte identity.

OPC identity requires co-expression of PDGFRA (growth factor receptor for PDGF-AA mitogen), OLIG2 (oligodendrocyte lineage TF), and SOX10 (neural crest/glial TF). All three are required for OPC identity.
MBP (myelin basic protein) is expressed upon OPC differentiation into mature myelinating oligodendrocytes. Its presence indicates the cell has exited the OPC state.
CSPG4 (NG2 proteoglycan) marks OPCs throughout the CNS and is the defining surface marker of the NG2-glia / OPC population.

Homeostatic microglia require co-expression of P2RY12 (purinergic receptor for surveillance), TMEM119 (microglial-specific transmembrane protein), and CX3CR1 (fractalkine receptor for brain residence). All three are downregulated in disease-associated microglia.
CCR2 marks blood-derived monocytes and infiltrating macrophages. Brain-resident homeostatic microglia do not express CCR2, distinguishing them from monocyte-derived macrophages.
TREM2 is a disease-associated microglia (DAM) marker that is expressed at low levels in homeostatic microglia. High TREM2 expression indicates transition to the DAM state.

Disease-associated microglia (DAM) are characterized by co-expression of TREM2 (triggers lipid phagocytosis) and SPP1 (osteopontin, a DAM effector). This circuit defines the DAM state in Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegeneration.
P2RY12 is a homeostatic microglia marker that is strongly downregulated during transition to the DAM state. Low P2RY12 is required for DAM classification.
APOE is strongly upregulated in DAM as part of the phagocytic lipid metabolism program. High APOE expression supports DAM identity.

Schwann cells co-express S100B (calcium-binding glial marker), MPZ (myelin protein zero, major PNS myelin component), and PMP22 (peripheral myelin protein 22). This trio is specific to PNS myelinating glia.
MBP is primarily a CNS myelin marker. Non-myelinating Schwann cells express very low MBP. High MBP would indicate CNS oligodendrocyte, not Schwann cell identity.

FOXJ1 is the master transcription factor for multiciliated cell identity. Ependymal cells lining brain ventricles are defined by FOXJ1 regulon activity, which drives ciliogenesis and motile cilium assembly.
TMEM212 (transmembrane protein) and CD24 are expressed in ependymal cells and mark the ciliated ventricular surface. Both are downstream of FOXJ1 activity.

TP63 (p63) is the master TF for basal keratinocyte identity. It maintains the basal stem cell program and is required for KRT14/KRT5 expression. TP63 regulon activity defines the basal keratinocyte state.
KRT14 and KRT5 form the keratin filament pairs specific to basal keratinocytes. Their co-expression marks attachment to the basement membrane.
KRT1 and KRT10 are expressed as keratinocytes transit from basal to spinous layer. Their co-expression marks suprabasal differentiation commitment.
KRT14 is a basal keratinocyte marker that is progressively downregulated upon basal layer exit. Low KRT14 in spinous cells reflects commitment to differentiation.
TP63 regulon activity is progressively silenced as keratinocytes exit the basal layer. Low TP63 activity is required for spinous layer identity.
Filaggrin (FLG), loricrin (LOR), and involucrin (IVL) are terminal differentiation markers expressed in granular layer keratinocytes. Their co-expression defines the cornified envelope program.
MITF is the master transcription factor for melanocyte identity. MITF regulon activity drives melanogenesis genes (DCT, TYRP1, PMEL) and is required for melanocyte survival and pigmentation.
DCT (dopachrome tautomerase), TYRP1, and PMEL (gp100) are MITF target genes required for melanin synthesis and melanosome biogenesis.
EPCAM marks epithelial cells. Melanocytes are neural crest-derived and do not express EPCAM despite residing in the skin epithelium.
CD1A (antigen presentation for lipids) and CD207 (langerin, a C-type lectin) define Langerhans cells. CD207 drives Birbeck granule formation, unique to Langerhans cells.
Dermal fibroblasts express COL1A1 (fibrillar collagen), PDGFRA (growth factor receptor), DCN (decorin, ECM proteoglycan), and THY1 (CD90, fibroblast surface marker).
ACTA2 (alpha-SMA) is expressed by activated myofibroblasts but not quiescent dermal fibroblasts. Low ACTA2 is required to distinguish dermal fibroblasts from wound-healing myofibroblasts.
Proximal tubule cells express SLC34A1 (NaPi2a, sodium-phosphate cotransporter), CUBN (cubilin, endocytic receptor), and LRP2 (megalin), which together mediate bulk reabsorption in the early nephron.
AQP2 is the principal water channel of the collecting duct principal cells. Its absence distinguishes proximal tubule from collecting duct cells in the kidney.
SLC22A6 (OAT1) is an organic anion transporter expressed specifically in the proximal tubule, mediating secretion of urate, drugs, and toxins.

SLC12A1 (NKCC2) is the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter defining the thick ascending limb (TAL). UMOD (uromodulin/Tamm-Horsfall protein) is the most abundant urinary protein, exclusively expressed in TAL.
The thick ascending limb is impermeable to water. AQP2 absence is required; its presence would indicate collecting duct, not TAL.
SLC12A3 (NCC, thiazide-sensitive cotransporter) is the defining transporter of the distal convoluted tubule. CALB1 (calbindin D28k) marks DCT2 and is required for calcium reabsorption.

Collecting duct principal cells express AQP2 (apical water channel, AVP-regulated), AQP3 (basolateral water channel), and SCNN1A (alpha-ENaC, sodium channel). This trio enables regulated water and sodium reabsorption.
ATP6V1B1 is the B1 subunit of vacuolar H+-ATPase expressed in intercalated cells. Its presence contradicts principal cell identity.

Type A intercalated cells secrete protons via apical H+-ATPase (ATP6V1B1) and reabsorb bicarbonate via basolateral SLC4A1 (AE1, anion exchanger). This machinery defines urinary acidification in the collecting duct.
SLC26A4 (pendrin) is the apical bicarbonate secretor expressed in type B intercalated cells. Its absence distinguishes type A (acid-secreting) from type B (base-secreting) intercalated cells.
AQP2 marks principal cells. Its absence is required for intercalated cell identity; principal and intercalated cells are mutually exclusive collecting duct populations.
SLC26A4 (pendrin) is the apical chloride/bicarbonate exchanger defining type B intercalated cells. It mediates net bicarbonate secretion and chloride reabsorption during metabolic alkalosis.
AQP2 marks collecting duct principal cells. Intercalated cells (both A and B) lack AQP2.
WT1 (Wilms tumor protein 1) is the master transcription factor for podocyte identity. WT1 regulon activity maintains NPHS1 and NPHS2 expression, which form the slit diaphragm filtration barrier.
NPHS1 (nephrin) and NPHS2 (podocin) form the slit diaphragm at foot processes. PODXL (podocalyxin) maintains the charge barrier. All three are podocyte-specific.
EPCAM marks tubular epithelial cells. Podocytes are specialized visceral epithelial cells that have undergone mesenchymal-like transition and do not express EPCAM.
Mesangial cells express PDGFRB (receptor for mesangial cell growth/expansion signals) and CALD1 (caldesmon, smooth muscle-like cytoskeletal protein for contractility).
AQP2 marks collecting duct principal cells. Mesangial cells are contractile intraglomerular cells and do not express AQP2.
NPHS1 is podocyte-specific. Mesangial cells are not podocytes and do not form slit diaphragms.
MYH7 (beta-myosin heavy chain, dominant in ventricle), TNNI3 (cardiac troponin I), and TTN (titin, giant sarcomeric protein) define ventricular cardiomyocyte identity.

MYH6 (alpha-myosin heavy chain) is the dominant isoform in atrial cardiomyocytes. Low MYH6 distinguishes ventricular from atrial cardiomyocytes. The MYH7-high/MYH6-low ratio is the defining isoform switch.
NPPA (ANP, atrial natriuretic peptide) is primarily expressed in atrial cardiomyocytes. Low NPPA distinguishes ventricular from atrial identity.
MYH6 (alpha-MHC, dominant atrial isoform) and NPPA (ANP, the atrial natriuretic hormone) are co-expressed in atrial cardiomyocytes and define atrial identity.
MYH7 (beta-MHC) dominates in ventricular cardiomyocytes. Low MYH7 is required for atrial identity; the MYH6-high/MYH7-low ratio defines the atrial isoform program.
Cardiac fibroblasts express TCF21 (master TF for epicardial-derived fibroblasts), DCN (decorin ECM proteoglycan), PDGFRA (growth factor receptor), and FN1 (fibronectin for ECM assembly).
ACTA2 (alpha-SMA) marks activated myofibroblasts. Quiescent cardiac fibroblasts express low ACTA2; high ACTA2 indicates myofibroblast activation during cardiac remodeling.
TNNI3 is a cardiomyocyte-specific marker. Its absence is required for cardiac fibroblast identity.
Endocardial cells are specialized endothelial cells lining heart chambers. They express CDH5 (VE-cadherin), PECAM1 (CD31), and NFATc1, which regulates valvulogenesis.
MYH7 marks cardiomyocytes. Endocardial cells are endothelial, not myocardial, and do not express cardiomyocyte sarcomeric genes.

Pericytes express PDGFRB (PDGF-B receptor for pericyte recruitment), RGS5 (G-protein regulator for vessel tone), and KCNJ8 (Kir6.1, potassium channel). This combination distinguishes pericytes from SMCs.
MYH11 (smooth muscle myosin heavy chain) is the contractile marker of mature vascular smooth muscle cells. Pericytes lack MYH11, distinguishing them from SMCs despite both wrapping blood vessels.
ACTA2 (alpha-SMA) is expressed at high levels in SMCs but only low levels in pericytes. This expression difference, combined with MYH11 absence, distinguishes pericytes from SMCs.
Arterial endothelium is defined by active Notch signaling (NOTCH4), high connexin 37 (GJA4) for arterial gap junctions, and CXCL12 for hemato-endothelial crosstalk.
APLNR (apelin receptor) marks venous endothelium and is absent from arterial endothelium. Its presence contradicts arterial identity.
Venous endothelial cells express APLNR (apelin receptor, activated by venous flow) and NR2F2 (COUP-TFII, nuclear receptor that suppresses arterial identity and establishes venous fate).
GJA4 (connexin 37) is an arterial endothelial marker. Low GJA4 in venous endothelium reflects suppression of arterial fate by NR2F2/COUP-TFII.
Capillary endothelium mediates gas/nutrient exchange. CA4 (carbonic anhydrase 4), RGCC (cell cycle regulator), and CD36 (fatty acid translocase) mark tissue-specific capillary exchange functions.
PROX1 is the master regulator of lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) identity. PROX1 regulon activity is required and sufficient to reprogram blood EC to LEC fate.
LYVE1 (lymphatic hyaluronan receptor) and PDPN (podoplanin) are PROX1 targets expressed on LEC surfaces and are required for lymph drainage function.
Tip cells at angiogenic sprout fronts express ESM1 (endocan, VEGF-induced), ANGPT2 (destabilizes pericyte contacts to enable sprouting), and high KDR (VEGFR2 for VEGF sensing).
DLL4 (delta-like 4) is the Notch ligand induced by VEGF in tip cells to laterally inhibit neighbouring stalk cells from also becoming tip cells. High DLL4 is a defining tip cell feature.
Vascular smooth muscle cells express the contractile machinery: MYH11 (smooth muscle myosin), CNN1 (calponin 1), and ACTA2 (alpha-SMA). This trio defines the differentiated contractile SMC phenotype.

FAP (fibroblast activation protein) marks cancer-associated fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. Its absence in VSMCs is critical for distinguishing SMCs from activated stromal fibroblasts in the tumor microenvironment.

Myofibroblasts are activated fibroblasts that co-express ACTA2 (very high, drives wound contraction), CNN1, and FAP (fibroblast activation protein, marks activated state). This combination defines myofibroblastic activation.
MYH11 (smooth muscle myosin) is the definitive SMC marker and is low/absent in myofibroblasts despite their high ACTA2. This is the key discriminator from vascular SMC.

Inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs) are characterized by high IL6 (pro-inflammatory cytokine, activated by IL-1 from cancer cells), CXCL12 (SDF-1, T-cell exclusion factor), and PDGFRA. iCAFs are the major immunosuppressive fibroblast population.

iCAFs are non-myofibroblastic. TGFβ from myCAFs suppresses the iCAF inflammatory program; conversely, low ACTA2 in iCAFs reflects non-myofibroblastic identity. ACTA2 high would indicate transition to myCAF.
myCAFs (myofibroblastic CAFs) are activated by TGFβ from cancer cells. They co-express ACTA2 (very high), MMP11 (stromelysin-3, ECM remodeling), and FAP (pan-CAF marker elevated in myCAF).
IL6 is the signature cytokine of iCAFs. TGFβ signaling in myCAFs suppresses IL-1/IL-6 axis, creating mutual exclusivity between iCAF and myCAF states.

Beta cell identity requires co-active MAFA (beta-cell maturation TF) and PDX1 (pancreatic/beta-cell TF) regulons. MAFA drives INS transcription; PDX1 maintains beta-cell identity and insulin gene promoter activity.
INS (insulin) is the hallmark secreted product of beta cells and the most abundantly expressed gene in mature beta cells.
GCG (glucagon) is the defining hormone of alpha cells and is mutually exclusive with insulin. GCG presence rules out beta cell identity — this is the most critical islet disambiguation.
SST (somatostatin) is the delta cell marker. Its presence would indicate delta cell identity, not beta cell.
Alpha cells express glucagon (GCG, the secreted hormone), ARX (homeodomain TF required for alpha cell differentiation), and MAFB (MAF family TF maintaining alpha cell identity).
INS (insulin) is the beta cell hormone and is mutually exclusive with glucagon. INS presence rules out alpha cell identity.
SST (somatostatin) is the delta cell marker. Alpha and delta cells are distinct populations.
SST (somatostatin) is the defining secreted peptide of pancreatic delta cells. Delta cells regulate both alpha (GCG) and beta (INS) cell secretion via paracrine somatostatin signaling.
Both insulin (beta cell) and glucagon (alpha cell) are absent in delta cells. Delta cells form a distinct third islet population defined by somatostatin secretion.
PPY (pancreatic polypeptide) is the sole defining hormone of PP cells (gamma cells), a rare fourth islet population primarily in the head of the pancreas.
PP cells are defined by absence of all three major islet hormones (insulin, glucagon, somatostatin) combined with high PPY. This four-way discrimination identifies them as the rarest islet cell type.

Acinar cells produce digestive enzymes: PRSS1 (trypsinogen 1, the major serine protease), CPA1 (carboxypeptidase A1), and AMY2A (amylase 2A). This enzymatic trio is exclusively expressed in acinar cells.
KRT19 is a ductal epithelial marker expressed in pancreatic ducts and biliary epithelium. Its absence distinguishes acinar from ductal cells.
Pancreatic ductal cells express KRT19 (biliary/pancreatic epithelial keratins), CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator for bicarbonate secretion), and MUC1 (mucin for duct lining).
PRSS1 (trypsinogen) is an acinar enzyme. Ductal cells modify but do not produce digestive enzymes. PRSS1 presence contradicts ductal identity.

Thyroid follicular cells are defined by TSHR (TSH receptor, drives thyroid hormone synthesis), TG (thyroglobulin, the thyroid hormone storage protein), and TPO (thyroid peroxidase, iodination enzyme). All three are required for thyroid hormone biosynthesis.
CALCA (calcitonin) is the marker of parafollicular C cells. Its absence distinguishes follicular cells (thyroid hormone-producing) from C cells (calcitonin-producing).
Parafollicular C cells are neuroendocrine cells that produce calcitonin (CALCA) for calcium homeostasis. CHGA (chromogranin A) marks their neuroendocrine identity.
TG (thyroglobulin) is exclusively produced by follicular cells for thyroid hormone storage. C cells are CALCA-secreting neuroendocrine cells and do not express TG.
CMPs retain CD34 expression and upregulate CSF1R (M-CSF receptor, myeloid commitment receptor). This CD34+/CSF1R+ state marks the myeloid branch commitment point.
GATA1 is the MEP/erythroid/megakaryocyte TF. Low GATA1 in CMPs distinguishes them from MEPs which are GATA1-high. CMP→MEP transition requires GATA1 induction.
MPO (myeloperoxidase) marks mature GMP and neutrophil-lineage cells. Low MPO in CMPs reflects early myeloid commitment before granulocyte specification.
GMPs express CSF1R (myeloid commitment) and acquire MPO (myeloperoxidase), the definitive marker of granulocyte/monocyte commitment. MPO expression onset marks GMP specification from CMP.
GATA1 drives erythroid/megakaryocyte fate. GATA1 and MPO expression are mutually exclusive, reflecting the bifurcation between GMP and MEP lineages from CMP.
MEP identity requires co-active GATA1 (erythroid/megakaryocyte master TF) and KLF1 (erythroid TF). Their co-activity drives MEP toward erythroid vs megakaryocyte fate based on FLI1 competition.
FLI1 is expressed in MEPs and competes with KLF1 for GATA1 interaction. High FLI1 biases MEPs toward megakaryocyte fate; FLI1 decline allows KLF1/GATA1 to drive erythropoiesis.
CSF1R marks myeloid commitment (GMP/CMP). MEPs have exited the myeloid branch and do not express CSF1R.
Megakaryocytes are polyploid platelet progenitors expressing ITGA2B (CD41, surface glycoprotein for platelet aggregation), PF4 (platelet factor 4), VWF (von Willebrand factor), and high GATA1.
HBA1 (hemoglobin alpha) is the defining product of erythroid cells. Low HBA1 distinguishes megakaryocytes from erythroblasts, despite sharing GATA1 high expression.
GATA1 is the master TF for erythroid differentiation. GATA1 regulon activity drives HBA/HBB globin gene expression and erythroid-specific programs (ALAS2, SLC4A1) during red cell maturation.

Erythroblasts express alpha-globins (HBA1, HBA2) and ALAS2 (delta-aminolevulinate synthase 2, rate-limiting enzyme for heme biosynthesis). This hemoglobin synthesis program defines erythroid identity.
MPO marks granulocyte/monocyte lineage. Erythroblasts and myeloid cells are mutually exclusive, reflecting GATA1 (erythroid) vs C/EBPα (myeloid) TF competition.

Plasmablasts are early antibody-secreting cells defined by co-active IRF4 (very high, drives plasma cell program) and PRDM1/BLIMP1 (represses B cell identity genes including PAX5). Both TFs are required for plasma cell commitment.

BLIMP1 directly represses PAX5 during plasma cell differentiation. CD19 and PAX5 are progressively downregulated as plasmablasts exit B cell identity. Their low/absent expression confirms plasma cell commitment.

SDC1 (CD138, syndecan-1) is the canonical plasma cell surface marker used clinically for multiple myeloma diagnosis. MZB1 (marginal zone B cell protein) is a plasma cell endoplasmic reticulum chaperone.

Progenitor-exhausted T cells (TPEX) co-express TOX (exhaustion master TF, induces epigenetic silencing) and TCF7/TCF1 (self-renewal TF, not yet silenced by TOX). This co-expression defines the stem-like exhausted state that responds to checkpoint blockade.
TPEX cells express SLAMF6 (Ly108, self-renewal marker) and moderate PDCD1 (PD-1), reflecting partial but not terminal exhaustion. SLAMF6 marks the progenitor pool.
HAVCR2 (TIM-3) is the terminal exhaustion marker absent from TPEX cells. High TIM-3 combined with TCF7 loss defines terminal TEX, distinguishing them from TCF7+ progenitor TEX.
Terminally exhausted T cells are defined by TOX (exhaustion TF) co-expressed with terminal exhaustion effectors: HAVCR2 (TIM-3), LAG3 (immune checkpoint), and ENTPD1 (CD39, adenosine pathway).

TCF7 (TCF1) is silenced by TOX-mediated epigenetic reprogramming in terminal TEX. TCF7 loss is required for terminal exhaustion state — its presence indicates TPEX, not terminal TEX. This was a key Phase 1 finding.
PD-1 (PDCD1) reaches its highest expression in terminally exhausted T cells, reflecting maximal coinhibitory receptor burden.

M1-like tumor-associated macrophages express IDO1 (immunosuppressive tryptophan catabolism), CXCL9, and CXCL10 (T-cell chemoattractants). This interferon-stimulated program is induced by tumor-derived IFN-gamma.
MRC1 (CD206, mannose receptor) is an M2-like scavenger receptor expressed in anti-inflammatory macrophages. Its absence in M1-like TAMs reflects incompatible TF programs (IRF5 vs IRF4).
M2-like TAMs express MRC1 (CD206, scavenger receptor), CD163 (hemoglobin scavenger, M2 marker), and VEGFA (pro-angiogenic factor). This program promotes tumor angiogenesis and immunosuppression.
IDO1 is an M1-like TAM marker driven by IFN-gamma signaling. M2-like TAMs are alternatively activated and do not express IDO1.

SPP1+ TREM2+ TAMs are a disease-associated macrophage subtype found in tumor niches and fibrotic tissue. SPP1 (osteopontin) drives tumor invasion, TREM2 regulates lipid/cholesterol homeostasis, CCL18 promotes immunosuppression.
SPP1+ TAMs are characterized by low MHC-II expression (HLA-DRA), making them poor antigen presenters. Low HLA-DRA distinguishes SPP1+ TAMs from professional antigen-presenting M1-like TAMs.

Tumor-enriched Tregs express FOXP3 (Treg master TF), ENTPD1 (CD39, adenosine immunosuppression), LAYN (layilin, tumor Treg marker), and IL2RA (CD25). This quartet distinguishes highly suppressive tumor Tregs from peripheral Tregs.
IL7R (CD127) is downregulated in Tregs as IL2RA (CD25) is upregulated. Low IL7R combined with high FOXP3 and IL2RA confirms Treg identity over conventional T cells.

Extravillous trophoblasts (EVTs) invade the decidua and remodel spiral arteries. HLA-G (non-classical MHC for maternal immune tolerance), ITGA5 (fibronectin receptor for invasion), and MMP2 (matrix metalloproteinase for ECM degradation) define invasive EVT identity.
CDH1 (E-cadherin) is expressed in villous cytotrophoblasts (VCT) but is downregulated during EVT differentiation as part of the epithelial-mesenchymal-like transition enabling invasion.

Syncytiotrophoblasts (STB) form the outer multinucleated layer of chorionic villi. CGB (hCG beta subunit, the pregnancy hormone), ERVFRD-1 (syncytin-2, fusogenic retroviral envelope protein for syncytium formation), and SDC1 (syndecan-1) define STB.
HLA-G is the invasive EVT marker. STBs are non-invasive and do not require HLA-G for immune tolerance — they instead induce tolerance through other mechanisms.
TFPI2 (tissue factor pathway inhibitor 2) is highly expressed in STBs and regulates fibrinolysis at the maternal-fetal interface.

Villous cytotrophoblasts (VCT) are stem/progenitor trophoblasts that fuse to form STB or differentiate to EVT. CDH1 (E-cadherin for epithelial cohesion), EGFR (EGF receptor for proliferation), and moderate TP63 define VCT progenitor state.
CGB (hCG) is the STB-specific hormone. Low CGB in VCT reflects uncommitted progenitor state before syncytium fusion.

Decidual NK cells (dNK) are specialized uterine NK cells that promote vascular remodeling. They express NCAM1 (CD56), ITGA1 (CD49a, tissue-resident NK marker), and KIR2DL1 (inhibitory KIR for HLA-C tolerance of EVT).
TRAC (T cell receptor alpha constant) marks T cells. dNKs are innate lymphocytes without TCR recombination — TRAC absence is required to distinguish dNK from T cell populations.
Peripheral cytotoxic NK cells are GZMB-high. dNKs have low cytotoxic potential and low GZMB, reflecting their remodeling rather than killing function in the decidua.

Mature adipocytes express PPARG (master adipogenic TF), ADIPOQ (adiponectin, adipokine secreted by adipocytes), and FABP4 (fatty acid binding protein 4, lipid transport). This trio defines the lipid-storing adipocyte program.
LPL (lipoprotein lipase) is expressed at high levels in adipocytes for triglyceride hydrolysis and fatty acid uptake from circulating lipoproteins.

Pre-adipocytes are adipogenic progenitors expressing PDGFRA (fibroblast growth factor receptor) and PREF1/DLK1 (preadipocyte factor-1, inhibitor of adipogenesis that is lost upon terminal differentiation).
ADIPOQ (adiponectin) is a terminal adipocyte marker absent in pre-adipocytes. Pre-adipocyte identity requires PREF1 high and ADIPOQ absent.

Adipose tissue macrophages express CSF1R (M-CSF receptor for tissue-resident macrophage maintenance), MRC1 (CD206, alternatively activated), and TREM2 (lipid-associated macrophage marker in metabolically stressed adipose).
Skeletal muscle fibers express fast-twitch myosin heavy chain MYH1, alpha-actinin ACTN2 (sarcomere cross-linking), and fast-type troponin T (TNNT3). This defines the mature skeletal myofiber program.
MYH7 (beta-myosin) dominates in cardiac muscle and slow-twitch skeletal fibers. Most fast-twitch skeletal fibers have low MYH7, distinguishing them from cardiac cardiomyocytes.
Muscle satellite cells are muscle stem cells expressing PAX7 (muscle stem cell master TF), CD34 (progenitor marker), and NCAM1 (CD56, marks quiescent satellite cells).
MYH1 marks terminally differentiated myofibers. Satellite cells are undifferentiated progenitors and do not express structural myosin.
Tenocytes are the primary cells of tendons and ligaments, expressing high COL1A1 (type I collagen), TNMD (tenomodulin, tenocyte-specific glycoprotein), and SCX (scleraxis, tendon TF).

Dopaminergic neurons express TH (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate-limiting enzyme for dopamine synthesis), SLC6A3 (DAT, dopamine transporter for reuptake), and NR4A2/Nurr1 (TF required for DA neuron differentiation and maintenance).
SLC17A7 (VGLUT1) marks glutamatergic neurons. Dopaminergic neurons are not glutamatergic, though some co-release glutamate — VGLUT1 high is incompatible with canonical DA neuron identity.

Cerebellar Purkinje cells express CALB1 (calbindin D28k, calcium buffer), PCP2 (L7, Purkinje cell-specific protein), and GRID2 (GluRdelta2, cerebellar synapse receptor). This trio is specific to Purkinje cells.
